newsitem.title: FRANCE: Deutsche Bank sees 55 pct chance of on time EMU.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Bank sees 55 pct chance of on time EMU.

text.p: Deutsche Bank chief economist Norbert Walter said on Wednesday he rated at 55 percent the chances of European economic and monetary union (EMU) starting on time on January 1, 1999.
The key obstacle beyond the Maastricht convergence criteria was German opposition to Italy and Spain joining in the first wave of EMU participants at that date.
"I do believe the chances for EMU to occur in 1999 are 55 percent and the chances of failure are 45 percent," Walter told a conference of the French association of corporate treasurers (AFTE).
Walter said the decision in 1998 on the qualifying countries would have to be taken by a qualified majority of three quarters of the 15 European Union countries.
"The problem will thus be, how do you arrive at a majority decision without including these countries (Italy and Spain)," Walter said.

Italy and Spain have both recently produced 1997 budgets designed to meet the Maastricht target of getting public deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 to qualify for EMU in 1999.

The ideal solution would be to convince them -- notably via the urgings of French President Jacques Chirac and German chancellor Helmut Kohl -- that they must wait for further economic convergence before joining the single currency zone.

Norbert said Italy could trade its vote in the decision making process against a promise that, within the framework of the future exchange rate mechanism governing relations between "ins" and "outs" of EMU, "there be an unlimited commitment to support the lira".
This is far from the desires of central banks in the hard core of European Union EMU contenders.
"They will be difficult talks in terms of economics and in terms of politics," Norbert said.
"If Kohl accepts Italy, that would be the end of the Kohl government," he said. "We have our performance and we have Kohl. Kohl is more important," he said, stressing Kohl's European commitment.

Walter said he really hoped monetary union would happen and underlined that discussion on the criteria or a postponement could result in a "derailing of the process" and that this would be tragic for Europe.
"Europe is closer to Yugoslavia than many people think," he said, adding that failure would push EU countries to turn inwards.
"It would be back to tribalism once again," he added.
